Each person says “Amen” aloud and binds himself. The public oath reaches where public law cannot.
events.uncertainty: Moses speaks in Moab, and the other points show places he names. Regions and traditional sites are approximate.

lds.text: The people answer “Amen” to each curse. What kind of wrong does verse 18 name?

events.title: Blessings and terrible curses
events.summary: If Israel listens to the LORD, blessings will overtake them. They will be blessed in city and field, in children, crops, and herds. The LORD will send rain, and they will lend and not borrow. If they do not listen, curses will overtake them. They will suffer sickness, drought, defeat, and loss of all they work for. A far nation whose language they do not know will besiege their towns. They will be scattered among the nations and find no rest. They will even be offered as slaves in Egypt, and no one will buy them.
events.detail: The blessings fill fourteen verses, and the curses fill fifty-four. Verse 47 gives the root of the curses in one line. Israel did not serve the LORD “with joyfulness” when it had “abundance of all things.” Verse 48 turns each good into its loss: hunger, thirst, nakedness, and lack. The chapter ends in Egypt, where the story of rescue began (verse 68). It warns a nation before it enters the land. It is not a rule for judging one sufferer.
events.uncertainty: Moses speaks in Moab, and the other points show places he names. Regions and traditional sites are approximate.

lds.text: Read the whole warning with care. Avoid using its suffering language to assign blame to someone in distress. What does verse 47 say Israel failed to do in a time of plenty?

events.title: The covenant assembly
events.summary: Moses gathers all Israel in Moab for a covenant beyond the one at Horeb. He recalls Egypt and forty years when their clothes did not wear out. Everyone stands before the LORD: leaders, men, children, wives, and foreigners. Even the woodcutter and the water carrier are there. The covenant is also made with those not present that day. No one who turns to other gods in secret will be pardoned. Later nations will ask why the land was ruined and hear the reason. Secret things belong to the LORD, and revealed things to Israel and its children.
events.detail: Verse 10 begins the list with heads, elders, and officers. Verse 11 goes on to little ones, wives, and foreigners in the camp. It ends with the lowest jobs: cutting wood and drawing water. All of them “stand today” before the LORD and enter the covenant. Verses 14–15 stretch it further, to people not yet born. So the covenant is not held only by leaders or fighting men. Verse 29 gives everyone the same task: do the words that have been revealed.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies inward loyalty and shared covenant identity. Who stands in the covenant assembly in verses 10–11?

events.title: Return and choose life
events.summary: When scattered Israel returns to the LORD, he will gather them. He will bring them back from the farthest places. He will change their hearts so they love him and live. The command is not too hard or too far away. It is not in heaven or across the sea. The word is very near, in their mouth and heart. Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse, before them. He tells them to choose life by loving the LORD and holding to him.
events.detail: Verses 12–13 answer two excuses before anyone makes them. The command is not up in heaven, and it is not across the sea. No one has to fetch it. Verse 14 says where it already is: “in your mouth and in your heart.” Moses has just spoken it, and they can repeat it. So the open question is not knowing but doing. Verse 19 names that step: “choose life.”

lds.text: The Church lesson compares these words with Lehi’s teaching about agency. The word is “very near to you” (verse 14). What choice does verse 19 set before Israel?

events.title: Joshua, the written law, and the song
events.summary: Moses is 120 and tells Israel he will not cross the Jordan. The LORD and Joshua will go before them, so they must be strong. Moses writes the law and gives it to the priests and elders. Every seven years, at the feast of booths, it must be read to everyone. Men, women, children, and foreigners are to hear and learn. The LORD tells Moses the people will turn to other gods after his death. Moses writes a song to stand as a witness against them. The book of the law is placed beside the ark.
events.detail: Moses is about to die, and the people who heard him will die too. Verse 9 puts the law in writing and in the priests’ care. Verses 10–11 set a fixed time to read it aloud: every seventh year. Verse 12 calls men, women, little ones, and foreigners to listen. Verse 13 adds the reason: children “who have not known” must hear it. Each new generation gets the words directly, not only by report. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools such writing needed.
events.uncertainty: Moses speaks in Moab, and the other points show places he names. Regions and traditional sites are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how a community can preserve its commitments when a leader changes. Who must hear the law read every seven years (verses 12–13)?

events.title: The Song of Moses
events.summary: Moses sings a song and calls heaven and earth to listen. He calls God the Rock, whose work is perfect and whose ways are just. God found Israel in a desert and carried it as an eagle does. He fed Israel with honey and oil from the rock. But Israel grew fat, kicked, and left the God who made it. It turned to strange gods, so God hid his face. Yet he will judge his people and have compassion when their strength is gone. The LORD then tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo, see the land, and die there.
events.detail: Verses 10–14 describe God feeding Israel: honey, oil, and the best of the field. Verse 15 shows what the feeding led to. The people “grew fat, and kicked,” like a well-fed animal that fights its owner. Then they left “the Rock” who saved them. Deuteronomy 8:12–14 warned of exactly this. The song gives Israel’s failure in advance, as a witness (31:19–21). Verse 36 still ends with compassion when their power is gone.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the rock image with Christ. Israel “grew fat, and kicked” (verse 15). Whom did it forget?

events.title: Blessings for the tribes
events.summary: Before he dies, Moses blesses the tribes of Israel. He says the LORD came from Sinai and loves the people. Moses gave them a law as the inheritance of all Jacob. He asks that Reuben live and that the LORD hear Judah. Levi keeps the Urim and Thummim and teaches the law. Benjamin rests in safety, and Joseph’s land is blessed with dew and deep water. Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher each get a saying. Moses ends: no one is like God, and Israel is saved by the LORD.
events.detail: Each tribe gets its own words, and the words differ widely. Levi has holy duties, Joseph rich land, Gad a lion’s strength. Verse 4 comes before all of them and names what they share. The law Moses gave is “an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.” Land will be divided by tribe, but this inheritance is held in common. In Genesis 49:5–7 Jacob cursed Levi’s anger. Here Levi is trusted with the Urim and Thummim (verse 8).

lds.text: How do Moses’s blessings compare with Jacob’s blessings in Genesis 49? What does verse 4 say all the tribes share?

events.title: Moses’s departure and Joshua’s leadership
events.summary: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and the LORD shows him the whole land. The LORD says this is the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses may see it but not cross over. Moses dies there in Moab, and no one knows his tomb. He was 120, with clear eyes and full strength. Israel weeps for him thirty days. Joshua is full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses laid hands on him. No prophet like Moses has risen since, whom the LORD knew face to face.
events.detail: The book ends with a death and a handover in the same breath. Verse 8 gives the people thirty days to weep. Verse 9 says Joshua is ready, “for Moses had laid his hands on him.” The people listen to him, so the work goes on. Verse 10 does not let Joshua replace Moses in honor. No prophet since has been known by the LORD “face to face.” The loss is real, and the people still have a leader.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Deuteronomy names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: LDS sources teach that Moses was translated. They describe this as a change without ordinary death. What does verse 9 say prepared Joshua to lead?

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time. Exodus 13:17 names a near road, “the way of the land of the Philistines.” The encyclopedia article lists that name for this coast road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time. Numbers 20:17 and 21:22 name “the king’s highway” east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

guides.title: Deuteronomy: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Memory needs daily practice
steps.text: Verse 5 asks for love with the whole person. Verse 6 says where the words must be: on the heart. Verse 7 turns that inward state into a daily habit with children. The four settings cover a whole day: sitting, walking, lying down, rising. No special place or teacher is named. Verses 10–12 show why the habit is needed: full houses make people forget. Verse 20 expects it to work, since the child starts asking questions.

steps.title: The king must live under the law
steps.text: Verses 16–17 limit three things a king might gather: horses, wives, and treasure. Verse 16 ties horses to going back to Egypt, which is forbidden. Verses 18–19 give him a task: copy the law and read it daily. Verse 20 states the aim: “that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers.” The king is called a brother and stays under the same law as everyone. First Kings 10:26–11:4 reports that Solomon broke all three limits.

steps.title: Small measures can cause real harm
steps.text: Goods were weighed against weights kept in a bag. Verse 13 pictures a cheat with two sets, one heavy and one light. The buyer has no way to test them. Verse 15 requires one “perfect and just” weight and measure. The reward promised is long life in the land, as for honoring parents (5:16). Verse 16 calls dishonest dealing an abomination to the LORD. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the rule has in view.

chapterMaps.narrative: Moses speaks to all Israel east of the Jordan in the fortieth year. He recalls how the LORD told them at Horeb to go and take the land. He recalls choosing leaders and judges to share his load. At Kadesh the people asked for spies, who brought back good fruit. Still the people refused to go up and said the LORD hated them. The LORD swore that generation would not see the land, except Caleb and Joshua. Moses says the LORD was angry with him too. The people then went up without the LORD and were beaten back.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel wandered around Mount Seir for many days. The LORD told them not to fight Esau’s people and to pay for food. He gave Moab and Ammon to Lot’s children, so Israel must leave them alone. Other peoples had also replaced earlier peoples in those lands. Thirty-eight years passed until the fighting men of the first generation died. Then the LORD gave Sihon the Amorite into Israel’s hand. Moses sent Sihon words of peace, and Sihon refused. Israel defeated him and destroyed his cities.

chapterMaps.narrative: Og king of Bashan comes out to fight, and the LORD gives him to Israel. Israel takes his sixty walled cities. Moses gives the land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Their fighting men must still cross and help their brothers. Moses tells Joshua not to fear the kingdoms ahead. Moses begs the LORD to let him cross and see the good land. The LORD refuses and tells him to look from the top of Pisgah. He must strengthen Joshua, who will lead the people over.

They must not forget Horeb, where the mountain burned and they heard a voice. They saw no form, so they must make no image of any creature. They must not worship the sun, moon, or stars. If they make idols, they will be scattered among the nations. Yet if they seek the LORD there with all their heart, they will find him. Moses sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan.

The people were afraid of the fire and asked Moses to listen for them. The LORD approved and wished they would always have such a heart.

These words must be on their hearts and taught to their children. They talk of them at home, on the road, at night, and at dawn. They are to tie them on hand and forehead and write them on doorposts. In the land they will have cities, houses, wells, and vineyards they did not make. Then they must not forget the LORD. When a son asks what the laws mean, the parent tells of slavery and rescue.

chapterMaps.narrative: Moses says the LORD will drive out seven nations greater than Israel. Israel is told to destroy them, make no treaty, and not marry among them. The reason given is that they would turn Israel to other gods. Israel must break their altars and burn their images. The LORD chose Israel, though it was the fewest of all peoples. He chose it because he loves it and keeps his oath to the fathers. If Israel obeys, he will bless its children, crops, and herds. The nations will be driven out little by little.

chapterMaps.narrative: Moses tells Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness. God humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna. He taught them that people do not live by bread alone. Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell. Now he brings them to a land of water, wheat, vines, olives, and metal. When they are full and rich, they must not forget the LORD. They must not say their own power got this wealth. If they forget and serve other gods, they will perish like the nations before them.

Israel must not say the land is a reward for its righteousness. The nations are driven out for their wickedness and because of God’s oath. Israel is a stubborn people, and Moses tells them to remember it. He recalls the golden calf, the broken tablets, and forty days of prayer. He names Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh. He prayed that God would remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and spare his people.

Aaron died, and the tribe of Levi was set apart to carry the ark. The LORD listened to Moses and did not destroy Israel. Now the LORD asks Israel to fear him, love him, and keep his commands. He owns heaven and earth, yet he set his love on their fathers. He takes no bribes and gives justice to the fatherless and widow. He loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner too.

It is a land of hills and valleys that drinks rain from the sky. The LORD’s eyes are on it all year. If Israel obeys, he will send early and late rain. If they turn to other gods, he will shut the sky. They must teach these words to their children and write them on their doorposts. Moses sets a blessing and a curse before them, on Gerizim and Ebal.

They are to bring offerings and tithes to the one place he will choose. There they eat and rejoice with sons, daughters, servants, and the Levite. They may kill and eat meat in any town, as they would a deer. But they must pour out the blood and not eat it. Holy gifts and vows still go to the chosen place. They must not copy the nations, who even burn their children for their gods.

If a brother, child, wife, or close friend secretly urges other gods, the same applies. The one who was urged must not hide it. If a town is said to have turned, the report must be checked with care. If it is true, the town is destroyed and burned. Nothing from it may be kept.

Camels, hares, pigs, and many birds are forbidden. Each year they eat a tenth of their crops at the chosen place. If the way is far, they may bring money and buy food there. They must not forget the Levite. Every third year the tithe is stored in their own towns. The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow come and eat their fill.

chapterMaps.narrative: Every seven years a creditor must cancel what a fellow Israelite owes. If Israel obeys, there will be no poor among them. They must open their hand to a poor brother and lend what he needs. They must not refuse a loan because the year of release is near. They must give freely, because there will always be poor in the land. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year. He must be sent away with gifts from flock, grain, and wine. Firstborn male animals belong to the LORD.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel keeps the Passover in the month of Abib, at the place the LORD chooses. They eat unleavened bread seven days, the bread of affliction. Seven weeks after harvest begins, they keep the feast of weeks with a free gift. They rejoice with children, servants, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows. They keep the feast of booths seven days after the harvest is in. Three times a year the men come before the LORD with a gift. Judges in every town must judge fairly and take no bribe. No sacred pole or pillar may stand by the LORD’s altar.

Hard cases go to the priests and the judge at the chosen place. Their verdict must be followed. Israel may one day ask for a king like other nations. He must be an Israelite whom the LORD chooses. He must not collect many horses, wives, or much silver and gold. He must write his own copy of this law and read it all his life.

A Levite from any town may come and serve at the chosen place. Israel must not copy the nations who burn children, tell fortunes, or consult the dead. The LORD will raise up a prophet like Moses from among them. Israel asked for this at Horeb, when they feared God’s voice. A prophet who speaks falsely in God’s name must die. If what a prophet says does not happen, the LORD did not say it.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel must set apart three cities in the land for anyone who kills by accident. An example is an ax head that flies off and strikes a neighbor. The cities keep the avenger from killing him in hot anger. If the land grows, three more cities are added. A man who kills from hatred is handed over to die. No one may move a neighbor’s boundary stone. A charge needs two or three witnesses, not one. A false witness receives the penalty he meant for the other person.

chapterMaps.narrative: Before battle a priest tells the army the LORD fights for them. Officers send home men with a new house, vineyard, or bride. They also send home anyone who is afraid. A distant city must first be offered peace. If it refuses, its men are killed and the rest are taken. Cities of the land itself must be destroyed, to keep Israel from their gods. During a long siege Israel must not cut down fruit trees. Only trees that give no food may be used for siege works.

textRoutes.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
textRoutes.summary: Moses speaks to all Israel east of the Jordan in the fortieth year. He recalls how the LORD told them at Horeb to go and take the land. He recalls choosing leaders and judges to share his load. At Kadesh the people asked for spies, who brought back good fruit. Still the people refused to go up and said the LORD hated them. The LORD swore that generation would not see the land, except Caleb and Joshua. Moses says the LORD was angry with him too. The people then went up without the LORD and were beaten back.
textRoutes.detail: Moses is speaking to the children of the people who refused at Kadesh. He says “you” throughout, as if they had been there (verses 26–27). The parents’ choice is told as the family’s own history. In verse 37 he adds his own loss: he also will not enter. He says it was “for your sakes,” tying his fate to theirs. Numbers 20:12 gives the reason as Moses’s own act at the rock. So the speech keeps the cost of the past in front of a new generation.
